slides.title: Multimodal Affect Recognition for Unseen Visitors in a Free-Roaming VR Museum
points: Akshaj Somanpura Rajendran
MSc Interaction Technology · Master's thesis defence
Supervisor: Shenghui Wang · University of Twente · 25 September 2026
slides.notes: Good morning. My thesis asks one question: can wearable sensors tell a museum guide how a visitor feels, second by second, for a visitor it has never met?

slides.title: Could a VR museum guide adapt to how you feel?
points: A guide that knows your **valence** (unpleasant to pleasant) and **arousal** (calm to excited) could stay longer at the works that move you
In VR the sensors come almost for free: an eye tracker in the headset, a wristband on the arm, a microphone
It has to work for a **visitor it has never seen**
So: how well can we recover valence and arousal, second by second, for an unseen visitor?
slides.caption: Valence and arousal as two axes of feeling
slides.notes: Affect here means two numbers: how pleasant, and how activated. A guide that could read them could adapt its story. VR gives us the sensors cheaply. The hard part is that a museum meets every visitor for the first time, so every result I show is for a visitor the model never saw during training.

slides.title: Prediction was the open step in the dataset's first thesis
points: **Van der Kaaden** collected this data to compare live and after-the-visit rating; prediction was a side analysis
His models learned a visitor they had seen (**0.84**) but fell near chance on a new one (**0.20 to 0.24**)
His future work: *“multimodal fusion, temporally finer feature representations, or settings with more clearly defined affective events”*
**This thesis takes that up** as the main question: prediction for an unseen visitor, with searched features, fusion, painting-level events and personalisation
And it explains the result, which a prediction study alone cannot
slides.notes: This dataset comes from van der Kaaden's thesis. His question was about the rating methods, and prediction was a side result: it worked for visitors the model had seen, and fell to near chance for new ones. In his future work he names exactly the next steps: multimodal fusion, finer features, and settings with clearer affective events, plus better cross-participant generalisation. That is the gap my thesis fills. I make prediction for an unseen visitor the main question, test each of those recommendations in turn, and add a way to explain why the result comes out as it does.

slides.title: A free-roaming visit past five paintings
points: **38 visitors** analysed: **22 rated live** with a joystick (rcea), **16 rated afterwards** from a replay (retro). The two are never mixed
Five sensor streams give **114 features per second**: pupil and gaze 7, skin conductance 10, heart 8, voice 88, words 1
**12,660 + 7,022** rated seconds, on a 0 to 10 scale
Every model is trained on all visitors but one and tested on the one left out
slides.caption: The five paintings (B1, B2, B3, C5, C6)
slides.notes: The data come from van der Kaaden's study in a VR version of the exhibition HERE: Black in Rembrandt's Time, made with the Rembrandthuis. Visitors walked freely. Some rated their feelings live with a joystick, others afterwards while watching a replay, and I keep those two streams apart because they measure affect differently. Each second becomes one row with 114 sensor features.

slides.title: Five experiments, each settling one choice
points: **1 · Each sensor alone:** clean the signal, pick its settings and the model
**2 · Sensors combined:** four ways to line up and merge them
**3 · Ordered levels:** low, mid, high instead of a 0 to 10 score
**4 · Paintings:** only the seconds a visitor looks at a painting, and where the variation in ratings comes from
**5 · Personalisation:** adapt the model to each visitor
Before comparing anything, I measured the noise: two runs of the same model differ by up to **0.08**, so smaller gaps cannot be told apart
slides.notes: The experiments build on each other: each one fixes a decision the next one uses. The score is the concordance correlation, CCC: 1 is perfect, 0 means the model knows nothing about that visitor. And I measured how much a score moves just from re-running the same model, 0.08, before any comparison, so I would not read noise as a result.

slides.title: No sensor, and no combination, rises above chance
points: All 20 sensor-by-slice scores lie between **-0.072 and +0.084** (0 = no information)
Eight model families and four alignment methods: all tied
Best combination = best single sensor: **+0.0822**
Ordered levels do no better: agreement is below chance on 3 of 4 slices
0 of 436 feature-rating correlations survive correction
slides.caption: Each dot is one held-out visitor; black bars are the means
slides.notes: This is the core result. Whatever I tried in the first three experiments, the score for a new visitor stays around zero. Individual visitors scatter both ways, which is why the means sit near zero. Even the raw correlations between features and ratings are not there before any model is fitted.

slides.title: The rating belongs to the visitor, not the painting
points: Which painting is viewed explains **0.1 to 1.5%** of a rating
Who is viewing explains **36 to 65%**
Two visitors at the same painting agree at almost zero (ICC 0.000 to 0.002)
A model trained on other people cannot know a new person's own level
Computed on the ratings alone, so it holds for any model
slides.caption: Crossed mixed-effects split of the ratings on attended seconds
slides.notes: To explain the null I split each rating into a part that belongs to the visitor, a part that belongs to the painting, and the rest. The painting part is tiny. Visitors looking at the same painting do not report the same feeling. That is why a model trained on other people has so little to go on, and it does not depend on which sensors or model I use.

slides.title: Focusing and personalising move in the right direction, but not enough
points: Training only on painting seconds: **0 of 48** paired tests show a gain
Personalisation moved the pooled scores the right way in **21 of 24** cells
A 3-minute labelled warm-up helps most, and on 3 of 4 slices more warm-up helps more
But no test survives correction (smallest q = 0.138), and the warm-up needs the visitor's own ratings
slides.caption: Adding the visitor's own first seconds to training
slides.notes: Restricting to painting seconds did not help. Personalisation is the natural remedy for a personal response, and the direction is encouraging: the more of the visitor's own ratings the model sees, the better. But with 16 to 22 visitors none of it is statistically established, and the best lever needs ratings a museum cannot ask for.

slides.title: What this means
points: Second-by-second affect could **not be recovered** for an unseen visitor in this collection
The reason is in the ratings: the response is **personal**, and very little of it is shared across people
So the next step is not a better model on the same data, but data designed so a shared response can be found
Limits: 22 and 16 visitors, a calm self-paced visit, wrist sensors while walking
slides.notes: So the answer to my question is no, not in this collection. The variance split tells me why: what visitors report belongs mostly to them, not to the painting. That points the next step at how the data are collected, not at a new model.

slides.title: How to make affect detection work
points: **Stimuli that provoke different responses:** more artworks, chosen for contrast, each seen more than once
**Anchor on shared moments:** compare visitors at a first look, a revisit or a guide remark, where affect is more likely present
**Personalise with few labels:** a short labelled warm-up folded into the headset's eye-tracker calibration, and label-free baselines
**Better labels and context:** one validated rating instrument, visitor background such as art familiarity, and logged scene luminance
**Run the variance split first** on a pilot's ratings, to check a shared response exists before building the sensor pipeline
slides.notes: Here is how I would make affect detection possible. First, choose artworks for the contrast in the responses they provoke, and let visitors see them more than once, so the shared part can be measured. Second, look at shared moments instead of arbitrary seconds. Third, personalisation came closest, so make the warm-up cheap by adding it to the calibration step the headset already has. Fourth, fix the labels and record who the visitor is and how bright the scene was. And before any of that, run the variance split on pilot ratings: it tells you whether there is a shared response to find at all.
